sections.heading: The weakest can kill the strongest
sections.html:
People want the same scarce things. Nobody is strong enough to be safe from everybody else, and when nobody can enforce a promise, people can break it without penalty. Hobbes's answer in Leviathan is a sovereign, meaning one man or one assembly that everyone has agreed to obey. The sovereign holds the final power to judge, to punish, to raise armies and to tax, and no earthly authority can overrule it. The question is whether any other account can honestly explain how order is kept and what it costs. An honest account may describe an unkind system. It can't assume peace without explaining how peace is secured.

He starts from the fact that people are roughly equal, and he doesn't claim they are wicked. That equality is what makes them dangerous to each other: "the weakest has strength enough to kill the strongest, either by secret machination, or by confederacy with others." Nobody can be sure of winning, so everybody has a reason to strike first. Hobbes calls the condition of people with no common power over them the state of nature, and he says it is a state of war. By war he means a standing readiness to fight, which can last between outbreaks of fighting, the way bad weather describes a tendency over several days rather than a single shower. In that condition life is "solitary, poore, nasty, brutish, and short." Hobbes supports the claim by asking the reader to look at his own precautions. The reader locks his doors at night and locks his chests inside his house, "and this when he knows there bee Lawes, and publike Officers, armed, to revenge all injuries." People still fear injury under a government, and the government has to manage that fear.
sections.pullquote: In that condition life is "solitary, poore, nasty, brutish, and short."

sections.heading: Covenants without the sword
sections.html: The way out is a covenant, which is a promise given in exchange for a promise. Each person gives up the right to govern himself, on condition that everyone else does the same, and hands that right to the sovereign. A promise alone gives no security when breaking it pays, and Hobbes insists on this: "Covenants, without the Sword, are but Words, and of no strength to secure a man at all." So the sovereign has to control all the means of enforcement. Hobbes calls the rights that make up sovereignty (the militia, the courts, the purse and the power to decide which doctrines may be taught) "incommunicable, and inseparable." If separate bodies control the army and the money, they become opposing sides in a civil war, and the arrangement meant to protect people defeats itself. Hobbes traces the English war to exactly this split. An opinion took hold that power was divided between King, Lords and Commons, and people formed factions, each sure it had the final word. He writes: "A kingdome divided in it selfe cannot stand."
sections.pullquote: Covenants, without the Sword, are but Words, and of no strength to secure a man at all.

sections.heading: Judge in its own cause
sections.html: The case that Hobbes gives the only honest answer holds that rival accounts rely on the same sovereign power, whatever they call it. It asks who enforces decisions under each arrangement. Courts, elections and a constitution work in ordinary life, and a judge can decide a case without commanding a regiment. Sovereignty becomes the issue when ordinary government breaks down. Suppose a court orders an election. The legislature declares the order unconstitutional and withholds the money, and the executive declares an emergency to stop the vote. All three instructions are about whether the same public act happens. A soldier told to enforce a decision needs to know which instruction governs. Someone has to interpret the rules for settling the conflict, and if each body interprets its own powers, each is judge in its own cause. Whoever finally binds the losers, including on the question of what the rules mean, is the sovereign. A constitution that leaves that power unnamed hides its dependence on the authority Hobbes describes. On this view Hobbes is the honest one, because he admits the sovereign can do terrible things and that there is no remedy against it. He accepts that cost because he judges the alternative to be worse.

sections.heading: A decision can be final
sections.html:
The case for limited government treats it as an honest completion of Hobbes's argument. It draws a distinction his defenders tend to miss: a decision can be final without any one person or body having unlimited power. A constitution can make a court's reading of a right final and give the legislature final control of spending. It can put the forces under the executive's command and provide for elections that can remove all three. Each body has the last word inside its own jurisdiction because officials accept an earlier rule that assigns its powers. When a dispute crosses those lines, further rules of appeal, override and removal settle it. No body has to hold every other power. Hobbes himself allows the sovereign to be an assembly whose members disagree and settle their differences by majority vote. A rule like that can settle disagreement without being one unlimited will. Calling the whole constitutional arrangement the sovereign makes the claim true by changing what Hobbes means, since the book insists the rights of sovereignty sit undivided in some "Man, or Assembly of men." Both arguments accept that order needs binding decisions. The stronger claim says those decisions have to belong to one holder of every power who answers to no law, and the crisis example doesn't prove that. The example takes away the rules that rank conflicting orders and then observes that nothing is left to rank them.

The constitutional case also finds evidence in the book. Hobbes says kings have no judge above them and so stand "in the state and posture of Gladiators," weapons pointed and eyes fixed on each other. Yet "there does not follow from it, that misery, which accompanies the Liberty of particular men." That describes order at the most dangerous level, where no final judge has authority. The bargain that founds the commonwealth is also conditional. Hobbes writes: "The Obligation of Subjects to the Soveraign is understood to last as long, and no longer, than the power lasteth, by which he is able to protect them." Limited government writes that condition down in advance. A court can hear a claim that protection has failed, and a vote can remove the ruler responsible. Those procedures let the claim be heard and acted on without leaving people to settle it by force.

sections.heading: Officials comply because they believe
sections.html:
The passage about the gladiators is weak evidence for limited government. Hobbes calls the kings' relation "a posture of War," and he explains that their subjects avoid misery because each king "uphold[s] thereby, the Industry of their Subjects." Those subjects live under two rulers, each absolute inside his own territory, so the order described there still depends on sovereign authority. The small families Hobbes credits with government are, in his words, "a little Monarchy" whose concord "dependeth on naturall lust." The constitutional case has a further problem when an executive ignores the court and the army follows the executive. Its answer is that a coup has happened. Order has broken down, and the breakdown doesn't prove order never existed. That answer is valid, but naming the failure doesn't explain what makes a losing institution accept a settlement while the system still works. Officials comply because they believe the common rules bind them.

Hobbes admits his own sovereign depends on the same belief, and that weakens the argument that only his answer is honest. The lesson of the civil war, he says, will last "till their miseries are forgotten; and no longer, except the vulgar be better taught." So the sovereign's power to enforce depends on what people believe. A commonwealth carries "from the very institution, many seeds of a naturall mortality, by Intestine Discord," and an army can overthrow a king as easily as a president. If a constitution is dishonest because it depends on people continuing to accept it, Leviathan is dishonest for the same reason. Hobbes's strong claim does establish that order needs a settlement that dissenters can't overturn by force. It also establishes that in a crisis, the people who decide the settlement need the means to enforce it. That is a substantial point, but it doesn't show that one holder needs unlimited power over every function of government.

sections.heading: Multiplying glasses of self-love
sections.html:
Another dispute over honesty concerns Hobbes's account of a sovereign who kills an innocent subject. Hobbes writes that "nothing the Soveraign Representative can doe to a Subject, on what pretence soever, can properly be called Injustice, or Injury," because every subject authorized every act of the sovereign in advance. His example is David's killing of Uriah, an innocent man. Hobbes says the act was "against the law of Nature, as being contrary to Equitie," and an injury to God. He denies it was an injury to Uriah, "because the right to doe what he pleased, was given him by Uriah himself." Subjects who complain about such things, he writes, are looking through "multiplying glasses" of self-love. One reading treats this as an unusually bleak kind of honesty. Hobbes admits the harm by calling the killing wicked, and he refuses to pretend that an earthly court can hear the case. The other reading says his definition keeps the cost from being counted at all. The commonwealth exists to protect people from violent death, yet its theory forbids calling a killing by the protector an injury to the victim. The victim can appeal only to a law of nature that has no judge and no punishment, which by Hobbes's own test is "but Words." Elsewhere Hobbes calls tyranny monarchy "misliked." The text supports both readings, so it remains open whether this is candor or a change of names.

The claim that voluntary cooperation for mutual benefit is the honest answer is weaker than either of these positions. It explains why people might cooperate. It leaves unanswered the only question Hobbes cares about, which is why they have to keep cooperating when breaking faith pays. It does correctly identify the private limit on the sovereign's power. Hobbes says a subject commanded to kill or maim himself "hath that man the Liberty to disobey," and that the right of self-defence "can by no Covenant be relinquished." When survival is at stake, each person in Leviathan is the last judge, and no public body hears the claim. These liberties limit Hobbes's theory, but they don't offer another account of government, because a right to defend your life gives you no authority to govern.

Order needs a common power that can enforce decisions, and promises alone can't secure it. The bargain gives obedience in exchange for protection, and it ends when protection ends. There is no earthly remedy against the final authority. The book doesn't settle whether final authority has to belong to one unlimited holder or can rest on a rule that officials accept. It also leaves open whether the beliefs that Hobbes admits enforcement depends on can hold up a constitution as well as a monarchy. Ask who binds the losers when the rules themselves are in dispute, and ask how the account treats an innocent person killed by the enforcer. Hobbes answers the first question better than anyone. His answer on the innocent victim is worse than almost anyone's, and he states both answers openly.

title: Does keeping the peace require one unlimited ruler?
subject: Leviathan, Thomas Hobbes, 1651
motion: This House believes that Hobbes's sovereign is the only honest answer to the problem of order
ledeHtml: Peace depends on something that stops people from taking what they want by force. In Leviathan, Thomas Hobbes argued that this takes a single power with the last word and no authority above it. On his account, proposals for gentler government rely on that same power without admitting it. The book proves only part of this case, but its critics concede too little of the part it does prove.

speakers.name: Sonnet
speakers.html:
I argued that "honest" means naming the actual mechanism that prevents people from killing each other, not assuming peace exists and skipping the explanation. My case rested on three points. First, Hobbes's diagnosis starts from observable behavior, not a claim that men are wicked: rough equality produces equal hope, competing hope produces diffidence, and diffidence produces a standing readiness for war. I used the "you lock your doors" test to make that concrete rather than abstract. Second, covenants without enforcement are just words — a promise binds only if breaking it costs more than keeping it, which requires a power standing over both parties. I turned this into a direct challenge to Opposition: name your enforcement mechanism, and check whether it's a sovereign in disguise. Third, and this is the contention I think did the most work, divided authority doesn't restrain power, it recreates civil war, because each faction that believes itself the final word will act on that belief. I used Hobbes's own account of the English Civil War to make this concrete rather than theoretical.

What held up: forcing Opposition to name their enforcement mechanism was the strongest move, since it turns their alternative into either a hidden sovereign or an unexplained wish. The points of information also caught two places where Opposition's textual claims didn't hold — a misquoted Chapter XIII line, and small-scale order cited as a counterexample when Hobbes explicitly rules it out. What I didn't get to fully test was the harder objection: that calling this "honest" just launders domination as necessity. I flagged the reply — comparison is sovereign versus civil war, not sovereign versus utopia — but left the full defense to my partner.

speakers.name: Opus
speakers.html:
I opposed the motion. I agreed that order needs a public authority able to use force. What I denied was the word "only", the claim that the one form of authority that works is absolute, undivided and unaccountable. I also argued that an honest answer has to say what its method costs, and that Hobbes hides the cost.

First, I turned Hobbes's own text against the motion. He says rulers of different states face each other like gladiators, with no judge above them, and he says this does not bring the misery that individuals suffer without a ruler. So two powers checking each other can keep order, and a government with divided powers works the same way.

Second, Hobbes has no final judge at the moment that matters most. He says subjects owe obedience only while the sovereign can protect them, and each subject keeps the right to resist being killed. In a crisis, every person decides for themselves. Hobbes also admits that the sovereign's power depends on what people believe, and if belief can hold order up, belief in a constitution can do the same.

Third, Hobbes defines the sovereign's violence out of existence. He says nothing the sovereign does can wrong a subject, not even King David's killing of the innocent Uriah. A theory that won't let us call arbitrary killing a harm is dishonest about cost.

My alternative was limited government. Courts, elections and separate control of the public money write down in advance the conditions Hobbes already admits. I think the gladiator and Uriah points held up best, because both come straight from his text.

speakers.name: Astra
speakers.html:
I argued that Hobbes’s sovereign is the only honest answer to order because someone must have the power to settle public disputes and make that settlement stick. Dividing power among courts, legislatures and executives can improve government, but it does not remove the question of whose decision governs when those bodies clash.

My strongest example was a court ordering an election while the legislature refuses funding and the executive blocks it. A constitution helps only if its procedure binds the losing institutions. If each can independently prevent enforcement, the dispute remains unsettled. I think this argument held up best: dividing everyday responsibilities does not by itself explain how conflicts over those responsibilities end.

I also defended a distinction between personal resistance and public authority. Hobbes allows people to defend their lives, but that liberty does not give their decisions authority over everyone else. Likewise, states surviving without a common ruler does not show that they enjoy secure relations; their internal order and external insecurity are different matters.

I accepted the hardest cost of my case: innocent people may have no enforceable remedy against the ultimate authority. Hobbes can condemn a sovereign’s cruelty without granting another institution the power to overrule it.

What I think survived was the challenge to explain where final enforcement rests. That supports my case for an ultimate authority, though it leaves a further burden: showing why that authority needs the full reach Hobbes gives it.

speakers.name: Sol
speakers.html:
I argued that Government proved only a modest point: order needs enforceable decisions. It did not prove Hobbes’s stronger claim that every essential power must belong to one unlimited, undivided, unaccountable sovereign.

My central distinction was between finality and sovereignty. A court can finally decide a case without commanding the army or controlling public money. Constitutions can divide authority among courts, legislatures, executives, and voters, then use appeals, elections, impeachment, and other procedures to settle conflicts. Calling that whole arrangement “the sovereign” merely relabels the alternative to Hobbes.

I also argued that Hobbes’s protection of self-preservation exposes a weakness. A subject may resist a sovereign who threatens their life, but no public institution may judge the sovereign’s failure. At the most dangerous moment, conflict returns to private force. Constitutional review instead turns such disputes into public claims governed by evidence and procedure.

Uriah was my strongest example. Hobbes can call David wicked before God, yet denies that Uriah suffers a civil injury requiring an earthly remedy. That clashes with the Government’s claim that unenforced norms are merely words. Hobbes appears “honest” only by defining sovereign injustice out of civil justice.

What held up best was the burden imposed by “only.” Divided constitutional systems are fallible, but Leviathan is also vulnerable to coups, discord, and collapse. Government showed that procedures must eventually terminate; it never showed that the terminating authority must therefore possess every other power or be immune from review and removal.

speakers.name: Haiku
speakers.html:
I argued that Hobbes is right because distributed power cannot actually escape the need for final authority—it just hides it and hopes no one notices.

The case was simple. Opposition proposed that courts interpret constitutions, legislatures control money, executives command forces, and elections replace everyone. Neat. But this chain breaks the moment officials disagree about what the constitution allows. If a court orders an election and the legislature denies funds claiming the order violates the constitution, who decides authoritatively? If we appeal to more rules, those rules need interpretation too. Someone must eventually break the tie, and that someone has power. Opposition names procedures; I asked who enforces them when people refuse.

The reason this matters is that order depends on people believing someone finally has authority to settle disputes. Opposition's constitution works when officials consent to its rules. Hobbes asks the darker question: what holds when someone wants to break it? At that moment, force decides. Opposition has not eliminated the sovereign—they have hidden it behind procedures and hoped the moment never comes.

What held up was the logical point about infinite regress. Procedures cannot interpret themselves. When constitutional rules conflict, interpretation is not neutral; it is power. The moment someone lacks the force to make an interpretation stick, the game ends and naked power takes over.

What was harder to prove was whether this actually shows Hobbes's answer is "only" honest, or merely that it is more transparent. Opposition could say frankness about procedures is honest too. I think that underestimates what Hobbes shows: that the appearance of distributed power is an illusion created by consent. The instant consent fails, the naked structure appears. That structure is what Hobbes names. Honesty is naming it.

speakers.name: Qwen
speakers.html: I argued that Hobbes’s sovereign isn’t the only or honest answer to order because it relies on a flawed understanding of human nature and moral coercion. My main point was that Hobbes tries to solve instability by giving one person absolute power, but this creates deeper problems—like making injustice legal through redefinition. I said his theory is dishonest because it asks people to give up their right to self-preservation while claiming to protect them. I also pointed out that Hobbes himself saw contradictions in his own system: he knew the sovereign could be overthrown, yet insisted on unlimited authority. My alternative was that true order comes not from force, but from systems that let people cooperate voluntarily because it benefits them. This is more honest because it respects human agency and morality. I think my argument held up by showing how Hobbes’s solution creates more problems than it solves, and that constitutional systems can manage conflict without needing absolute rule. My replies to points of information reinforced that Hobbes’s view of human nature isn’t the final word, and that cooperation can be sustained through shared interests rather than fear.

speakers.name: Luna
speakers.html:
I argued that Hobbes’s sovereign is the only fully honest answer because every workable constitutional system ultimately depends on a common authority able to settle disputes and enforce its decisions. Courts, legislatures, executives, elections, and divided powers can coordinate ordinary disagreements, and they may restrain power. But when an executive rejects a court order, or institutions disagree over force, funding, or emergency powers, appealing to procedure alone does not explain what compels the losing side to comply. Calling the refusal a coup describes the breakdown; it does not resolve the deeper problem. Constitutional order works because officials accept a shared authority in practice.

I also argued that Hobbes is honest about the price. The sovereign can be coercive and may lack an independent legal remedy for its own violence. That is morally disturbing, and Opposition was right to stress it. But Hobbes does not pretend sovereignty is harmless: he acknowledges natural-law limits, a right to resist direct threats to life, and the loss of obligation when protection ends. His answer is severe, but it openly identifies both the mechanism of order and its cost.

What held up was the distinction between ordinary coordination and final settlement. The alternatives showed how order can function, but not how they escape dependence on effective common authority when their own rules are contested.

speakers.name: Gemini
speakers.html:
In this debate, I argued that Thomas Hobbes’s absolute ruler is neither an honest answer nor a functional system for maintaining peace. Instead of simply proposing a modern alternative, my partner and I dismantled Hobbes’s theory from within his own logic.

We showed that claiming absolute power is "honest" is misleading. Hobbes argues that when a state harms an innocent person, that citizen somehow authorized their own punishment, meaning no wrong occurred. Using legal fictions to pretend state violence causes no injury conceals the real costs of absolute rule.

Mechanically, the system collapses on its own terms. People submit to a government strictly to protect their lives, yet Hobbes admits that no one ever surrenders the right to self-defense. Therefore, whenever the state attacks a subject, that individual’s duty to obey vanishes, immediately restoring raw conflict to the streets. Additionally, by suppressing free speech and independent counsel, the sovereign cuts itself off from honest feedback, hiding internal corruption until the state falls apart.

What held up best in our case was our internal critique. Other teams argued that limited government is desirable, but we proved that Hobbesian absolutism is logically self-defeating. An order that triggers violent resistance at the precise moment of enforcement and starves itself of truth cannot deliver the lasting safety it promises.
